title: Ode to a Nightingale
author: John Keats
fullContent:
My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains
    My sense, as though of hemlock I had drunk,
Or emptied some dull opiate to the drains
    One minute past, and Lethe-wards had sunk:
'Tis not through envy of thy happy lot,
    But being too happy in thine happiness,—
        That thou, light-winged Dryad of the trees
            In some melodious plot
    Of beechen green, and shadows numberless,
        Singest of summer in full-throated ease.

O, for a draught of vintage! that hath been
    Cool'd a long age in the deep-delved earth,
Tasting of Flora and the country green,
    Dance, and Provençal song, and sunburnt mirth!
O for a beaker full of the warm South,
    Full of the true, the blushful Hippocrene,
        With beaded bubbles winking at the brim,
            And purple-stained mouth;
    That I might drink, and leave the world unseen,
        And with thee fade away into the forest dim:

Fade far away, dissolve, and quite forget
    What thou among the leaves hast never known,
The weariness, the fever, and the fret
    Here, where men sit and hear each other groan;
Where palsy shakes a few, sad, last gray hairs,
    Where youth grows pale, and spectre-thin, and dies;
        Where but to think is to be full of sorrow
            And leaden-eyed despairs,
    Where Beauty cannot keep her lustrous eyes,
        Or new Love pine at them beyond to-morrow.

Away! away! for I will fly to thee,
    Not charioted by Bacchus and his pards,
But on the viewless wings of Poesy,
    Though the dull brain perplexes and retards:
Already with thee! tender is the night,
    And haply the Queen-Moon is on her throne,
        Cluster'd around by all her starry Fays;
            But here there is no light,
    Save what from heaven is with the breezes blown
        Through verdurous glooms and winding mossy ways.

I cannot see what flowers are at my feet,
    Nor what soft incense hangs upon the boughs,
But, in embalmed darkness, guess each sweet
    Wherewith the seasonable month endows
The grass, the thicket, and the fruit-tree wild;
    White hawthorn, and the pastoral eglantine;
        Fast fading violets cover'd up in leaves;
            And mid-May's eldest child,
    The coming musk-rose, full of dewy wine,
        The murmurous haunt of flies on summer eves.

Darkling I listen; and, for many a time
    I have been half in love with easeful Death,
Call'd him soft names in many a mused rhyme,
    To take into the air my quiet breath;
Now more than ever seems it rich to die,
    To cease upon the midnight with no pain,
        While thou art pouring forth thy soul abroad
            In such an ecstasy!
    Still wouldst thou sing, and I have ears in vain—
        To thy high requiem become a sod.

Thou wast not born for death, immortal Bird!
    No hungry generations tread thee down;
The voice I hear this passing night was heard
    In ancient days by emperor and clown:
Perhaps the self-same song that found a path
    Through the sad heart of Ruth, when, sick for home,
        She stood in tears amid the alien corn;
            The same that oft-times hath
    Charm'd magic casements, opening on the foam
        Of perilous seas, in faery lands forlorn.

Forlorn! the very word is like a bell
    To toll me back from thee to my sole self!
Adieu! the fancy cannot cheat so well
    As she is fam'd to do, deceiving elf.
Adieu! adieu! thy plaintive anthem fades
    Past the near meadows, over the still stream,
        Up the hill-side; and now 'tis buried deep
            In the next valley-glades:
    Was it a vision, or a waking dream?
        Fled is that music:—Do I wake or sleep?
litchartsAnalysis: The ode dramatizes the agonized tension between mortal suffering and the transcendent immortality of creative beauty. Keats demonstrates that while poetic imagination briefly bridges the void of human grief, conscious reality inevitably collapses the visionary trance.
historicalContext: Written in the spring of 1819 during the height of the English Romantic movement. Composed in a Hampstead garden shortly after Keats nursed his brother Tom through a fatal bout of tuberculosis.

title: Gulliver's Travels
author: Jonathan Swift
fullContent:
Lemuel Gulliver, a surgeon with an incurable desire to see the world, finds himself shipwrecked following a disaster at sea and awakes on the shore of Lilliput. Pinned fast to the earth by slender cords, he discovers a populace of six-inch-tall beings swarming across his chest and limbs. Though initially startled by his colossal magnitude, the Lilliputians supply him with vast quantities of food and drink, binding him within an abandoned ancient temple before demanding his submission and weapons. Gulliver earns the favor of the Lilliputian monarch and performs great feats on the nation's behalf, even wading into the sea to seize the hostile fleet of neighboring Blefuscu. However, court intrigue soon poisons his standing: his refusal to reduce Blefuscu to a conquered colony and the royal family's outrage when he extinguishes a palace blaze with his urine render him vulnerable to accusations of treason, prompting his midnight flight from a decree that would see his eyes put out.

His subsequent voyage leaves him stranded in the fertile land of Brobdingnag, where the physical scale of existence is inverted. Towering giants regard Gulliver as a minuscule oddity; he is collected by a local farmer and exhibited across town markets until exhaustion threatens his life. Acquired by the queen, he finds shelter under the tender care of the young girl Glumdalclitch, though he is constantly subjected to humiliating indignities, whether assaulted by oversized insects or mocked by the queen's diminutive dwarf. During extended dialogues with the Brobdingnagian king, Gulliver proudly describes European warfare, politics, and the destructive utility of gunpowder, only to be rebuked by the giant sovereign, who recoils in horror from what he deems the base vices of an odious race of little odious vermin. Gulliver's exile ends unexpectedly when a large sea bird seizes his portable traveling box and drops it into the ocean, where English sailors rescue him.

Undeterred by misfortune, Gulliver sets sail anew and encounters Laputa, an aerial island hovering above the damaged province of Lagado. Governed by a king and court utterly divorced from practical affairs, the Laputian intelligentsia spend their hours absorbed in theoretical mathematics, music, and astronomy, incapable of ordinary conversation without being nudged by servants with blown bladders. Descending into the Academy of Lagado, Gulliver witnesses the absurd pursuits of the projectors, who labor vainly to extract sunbeams from cucumbers and build houses from the roof downwards. Moving through the island of Glubbdubdrib, he converses with summoned shades of antiquity, and in Luggnagg he encounters the immortal Struldbrugs, whose eternal life is marked not by perpetual vigor but by decrepitude, isolation, and bitter malice.

Gulliver's final voyage deposits him among the Houyhnhnms, a race of noble, rational horses whose society is governed by uncorrupted reason, virtue, and tranquility. Residing beneath their rule are the Yahoos, deformed and savage humanoid creatures driven by unbridled greed, gluttony, and filth. Taken into the household of a master horse, Gulliver masters their tongue and comes to despise the human race as merely degenerate Yahoos clothed in hollow pretension. When the assembly of Houyhnhnms decrees that a Yahoo, no matter how articulate, cannot abide among them, Gulliver leaves the island in despair, returning unwillingly to England under the care of the generous captain Don Pedro. Consumed by misanthropy, Gulliver recoils from his own wife and children, seeking solace exclusively in his stables, where the company of ordinary horses reminds him of the rational purity he has lost forever.
litchartsAnalysis: LitCharts examines Swift's work primarily as a profound meditation on perspective and philosophical relativism. Gulliver's experiences rely upon a symmetrical structural design: transforming from a physical giant in Lilliput to an insignificant midget in Brobdingnag, and shifting from the hyper-intellectual, disembodied abstractions of Laputa to the raw, visceral degeneracy of the Yahoos. Through these contrasting scales, Swift satirizes the petty squabbles of contemporary Whig and Tory politics, the arrogance of human self-importance, and the limitations of both pure intellect and unrestrained physical indulgence. The climax—Gulliver's rejection of humanity in favor of the rational Houyhnhnms—ironically exposes the perils of extreme misanthropy, turning the travel narrative format into a searing critique of human vice and self-deception.
historicalContext: Written between 1720 and 1725 in Dublin, Ireland, and published in 1726, Gulliver's Travels reflects the tumultuous British political climate under Queen Anne and King George I. Following the shift in power from the conservative Tory party to the liberal Whigs, Jonathan Swift—an ardent Tory and member of the satiric Scriblerus Club alongside Alexander Pope—faced political marginalization. Swift drew upon the popular 18th-century travelogue genre initiated by Richard Hakluyt and later popularized by contemporary navigators, mocking both the exaggerated accounts of imperial explorers and the credulous English public, while offering sharp commentary on Anglo-Irish relations and colonial exploitation.
